text: Roller coasters are amusement rides designed for amusement parks and modern theme parks. Early versions in the 16th and 17th centuries, popular in Russia, involved wooden sleds sliding down large ice slides. The first roller coasters with trains attached to wooden tracks emerged in France in the early 1800s. While wooden roller coasters are still manufactured, steel roller coasters, introduced in the mid-20th century, have become more widespread and are found on every continent except Antarctica. Amusement parks often compete to build the tallest, fastest, and longest rides to attract thrill seekers and increase attendance. Ranked by height, speed, length, and number of inversions, roller coasters have frequently served as key attractions in this competition. Computer-simulated models have driven innovations that enhance thrill levels while improving quality and durability. The debut of Magnum XL-200 in 1989 at Cedar Point marked the first complete-circuit roller coaster to exceed 200 feet (61 m), representing a turning point in the industry. This period, known as the Coaster Wars, saw intense competition as parks raced to set world records, with some records lasting only a year or less. The Smiler features fourteen inversions, the highest number of any roller coaster. Former record holder Kingda Ka, which stood as the world's tallest coaster at 456 feet (139 m) since 2005, held its record until its closure in 2024. Formula Rossa, previously the world's fastest roller coaster, reaches a top speed of 149 mph (240 km/h). Steel Dragon 2000, once the world's longest at 8,133 feet (2,479 m), held its record from opening until the launch of Falcons Flight in 2025, which now holds the titles for tallest, fastest, and longest roller coaster. This listing includes all types of roller coaster inversions.
